title: How to Make SSO Work: Setup Steps and 2026 Costs
summary: To make SSO work, select an identity provider and configure integration. Find setup instructions and 2026 costs for different providers to compare.
body_markdown:
## Identify common SSO mistakes with published data


In the[Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report 2025, as summarised by Optery](https://www.optery.com/phishings-role-in-breaches-behind-the-numbers-of-verizons-2025-dbir/) , **stolen credentials started 22% of breaches** , which is why attackers go after them first.


Exploited flaws came next at 20%, and phishing at 16%. The gap between first and second is two points, so **SSO fixes one route without closing the others.**


### Avoid SSO lockout and expired certificates


Create a break-glass admin before you enable "require SSO": one local account, exempt from enforcement, with its password in a vault two people can open. Without it, a misconfigured identity provider locks out the very admins who would fix it.


Next, put the SAML signing certificate's expiry date in a calendar with an owner. When it lapses, every assertion fails validation and every login breaks at once.


Enforce only after a pilot group has signed in successfully, and check email attributes during the pilot. If the provider sends` j.smith@` and the app holds` john.smith@` , the app creates a second, empty account instead of matching the first.


### Offboarding without SCIM


Without SCIM, removing a leaver depends on someone remembering every app. SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) lets the identity provider create and disable app accounts automatically.


Zluri's figures, relayed by[NHIMG](https://nhimg.org/articles/it-offboarding-gaps-leave-former-employee-access-alive/) , show how that goes: **50% of former-employee accounts are still active** after more than a day, and 25% after a week or longer, meaning your company likely has active accounts belonging to people who no longer work there.


**Disabling someone in the identity provider doesn't end their sessions in the apps.** A 30-day session lifetime leaves a leaver's open browser logged in for up to a month.


> **Disabling someone in the identity provider doesn't end their sessions in the apps.


So set short session limits and require SCIM on the plan tier you buy. That's usually a higher tier than the one that merely offers SSO.


### Treating SSO as a replacement for MFA


When one identity-provider login is phished, every connected app opens with it, because SSO changes where the password lives without making it harder to steal.


Phishing alone accounts for 16% of breaches in the DBIR data above, which means it's a vector responsible for a large chunk of industry compromise.


Require multi-factor authentication at the identity provider, preferably phishing-resistant keys or passkeys, and treat that as part of the SSO project.


Admin visibility has limits here. A sign-in log tells you who authenticated and from where, but it won't tell you the person was the employee. A stolen session cookie looks like a normal login.
